items.summary: An interview introduction is not a biography. It is a short, structured answer that tells the interviewer who you are, why you are relevant and what you want next. After reading this you can prepare a 60-second introduction, describe your experience with evidence, ask questions that show judgement, and close the interview and follow up in a way that is remembered.
items.title: How to Introduce Yourself in a Job Interview

items.summary: A request for a raise is a business case, not a favour. It works when you arrive with evidence, a number and a calm plan. After reading this you will know when to ask, how to build the evidence, how to say the sentence out loud, and what to do in the week after you hear no.
items.title: How to Ask for a Raise Politely

items.summary: Competence shaming is a way of gaining standing by lowering somebody else's competence, and the difference from honest criticism is the aim, not the words. After reading this you can name the four moves of the attack, tell honest criticism from a status attack, answer one without escalating it, and notice when you are doing it yourself.
items.title: Competence Shaming and Status Manipulation

items.summary: An argument can be lost without a single false fact. When the ground moves — to the person, to the feeling, to a standard that changes after the facts arrive — the claim is never tested. After reading this you can name the nine moves, spot them in a live exchange, answer each one with one sentence, and keep your own argument clean when you are being pushed.
items.title: Psychological Manipulation in Arguments

items.summary: Gaslighting is the rewriting of a shared account until the person who was there doubts their own memory. After reading this you can tell a deliberate attack apart from an ordinary disagreement and an honest mistake, name the three moves of DARVO, recognise the pattern in plain language at work and at home, and answer it with sentences you can reuse.
items.title: Gaslighting and DARVO: Manipulating Perception and Turning the Blame Around

items.summary: Long-term singleness has a vocabulary of its own, and much of the trouble around it comes from using the wrong word. After reading this you can tell the state of being single from the story a person tells about it, name the words that describe it precisely, recognise the pressure underneath it, and answer the questions other people ask without apologising for the answer.
items.title: The Psychology of Long-Term Singleness

items.summary: The dating market is a metaphor, not a law, and hypergamy is a hypothesis that people still argue about. After reading this you can explain what the metaphor describes and what it assumes, name the words the subject uses, state what the hypothesis predicts and what it cannot explain, compare it with the other answers for the same pattern, and use the vocabulary without turning people into a ranking.
items.title: The Dating Market and the Hypergamy Hypothesis

items.summary: Emotions do not decide what you say next, and relationships run on rules nobody writes down. After reading this you can tell the difference between regulating a feeling and hiding it, describe what a partner sees when a feeling is suppressed, reappraised or rehearsed, name the expectations under a conflict, and use short sentences to ask for a pause, state a need and agree a repair.
items.title: Emotional Regulation and Relationship Expectations

items.summary: Power is the ability to make things happen; authority is power the other side accepts. After reading this you can tell the two apart, name the five bases on which authority is claimed, test whether a decision can be questioned, and raise an objection in a meeting, in a review or in writing without turning the difference into insubordination.
items.title: Power Dynamics and Authority Manipulation

items.summary: A gender role is a rule about what a category of people is expected to do. After reading this you can tell a role from a stereotype, name who enforces the rule around you, see how the cost of breaking it falls on one person, and negotiate a division of work at home or at work before the next crisis decides it for you.
items.title: Gender Roles and Social Expectations

items.summary: The biological clock is a phrase, not a device, and it mixes a real biological change with a social deadline. After reading this you can tell fertility, fecundity and the ovarian reserve apart, say what menopause and perimenopause name, explain where reproductive urgency and timeline pressure come from, and hold a conversation about timing without panic.
items.title: The Biological Clock and Reproductive Psychology

items.summary: Loneliness is a feeling, and being alone is a fact, and the two are easily confused. After reading this you can tell loneliness, isolation, alienation and solitude apart, explain why a standard rises and what a closed door costs, describe commitment as a series of small decisions, and say what you want from a relationship in sentences you can use.
items.title: Loneliness, Selectivity and Commitment

items.summary: Marriage timing is not one decision but a set of forces: work, money, study, family, law and the people around you. After reading this you can name the forces that push a date earlier or later, use the vocabulary of timing accurately, tell the peer effect from the family effect, and run a short procedure that separates the practical questions from the pressure.
items.title: The Psychology of Marriage Timing

items.summary: A currency is a promise, a code and a habit. After reading this article you can tell the name of a currency from its ISO 4217 code and its symbol, explain why one currency serves many countries, read a note and name its denomination and its minor unit, describe how a market, a taxi or a restaurant expects payment, and say what money means in the culture you work in.
items.title: The Currencies of 195 Countries: How They Are Used and What Money Means

items.summary: A number without a unit is not a measurement, and a formula whose two sides do not match in units is not a formula. After reading this you can name the seven base units, write a measurement the way a drawing expects it, check a formula with dimensional analysis, and explain why a converted number can be right in arithmetic and wrong in meaning.
items.title: Units, Dimensions and Dimensional Analysis

items.summary: Attachment styles describe the promises a person brings to a partner, the way they read availability, and what they do when a partner is unavailable. After reading this you can name the four styles, describe what each one looks for and fears, recognise the signals that switch your own pattern on, and say what you need in words your partner can act on.
items.title: Attachment Styles in Romantic Relationships

items.summary: An average difference between two groups says where the centres of two clouds sit, not where any one person stands. After reading this you can name the five parts of emotional maturity, say what a claim about men and women can and cannot tell you about one person, read a group claim without turning it into a rule, and hold a conversation about it without the argument becoming a fight.
items.title: Gender Differences in Emotional Maturity

items.summary: Mate selection is the process of choosing a partner, and it has its own vocabulary. After reading this you can separate attraction, preference and decision, describe how people actually choose, read the direction and the size of an age gap, and run a short check on the preferences you say you hold.
items.title: Mate Selection and Age Preferences

items.summary: Persuasion is ordinary in a negotiation; the dark part is using it to hide the real price, the real stock or the real deadline. After reading this you can name nine techniques, say what the honest version of the same request is, and prepare the two things that protect you: your alternative and your walk-away price.
items.title: Dark Psychology in Business and Negotiation

items.summary: English is one language with many accents, and most of the differences you meet are regular rather than wrong. After reading this you can recognise British, American, Australian, Indian and Singapore English by their vocabulary and grammar, understand why the differences exist, and choose the variety that fits your listener.
items.title: Why English Is Different Around the World

items.summary: Working from another country is now possible for tens of millions of people, but it is governed by visa rules, tax rules and the cost of daily life. After reading this you can tell a genuine digital nomad from a tourist working online, check what you must do before you move, and pick a city that fits your work and your budget.
items.title: Digital Nomads: Working From Anywhere

items.summary: Moving to a new country changes small things before big ones: greetings, meals, punctuality, silence. After reading this you can name what is surprising you, tell a personal habit from a local rule, and handle the first weeks without assuming that your way is the correct one.
items.title: Culture Shock: Things That Surprise People Abroad

items.summary: People meet each other less than they did twenty years ago, and the reason is not that they stopped liking each other. After reading this you can explain the forces behind it, tell loneliness apart from solitude, plan shared time that people actually attend, and keep a friendship alive across distance and full calendars.
items.title: Why People Are Spending Less Time Together

items.summary: An anti-lock braking system is often taken as a promise that the car always stops in the same distance. It is not. After reading this you can describe how the system works, explain where it does not help, choose between threshold braking, progressive braking and engine braking, brake well with or without ABS, and say what to do when the warning light comes on.
items.title: ABS Is Not the Absolute Truth: The Limits of Anti-Lock Braking

items.summary: Washing machines, dishwashers and ovens are labelled in pictures so they can be used in any country. After reading this you can name the common symbols, choose the right programme and temperature, understand the salt, detergent and rinse aid symbols, and work a machine you have never used before.
items.title: Understanding Household Appliance Symbols

items.summary: A breakdown is a conversation you will have while standing on a hard shoulder, so the words matter. After reading this you can make the scene safe, describe the fault in a way that gets the right help sent, say what you need, and look after the people around you until someone arrives.
items.title: What to Say When Your Car Breaks Down

items.summary: A food label tells you three things: what is inside, how much of it there is, and how long it is safe. After reading this you can read any label in any country, tell a use-by date from a best-before date, and decide at the shelf whether a product is worth buying.
items.title: Reading Food Labels and Expiration Dates

items.summary: A pump moves water, and a pump that moves water can also move current. After reading this article you can name the parts of a pump installation, explain where the leakage comes from, say how current reaches a person through wet ground, compare the six protections that guard the circuit, run a safe check on a pump, and give the right instructions in the first minutes after a shock.
items.title: Water Pumps and the Risk of Electric Leakage

items.summary: A water heater is a metal tank full of water with electricity inside it. After reading this article you can describe how a fault current reaches a person, name the parts that protect you, do the right things in the first minutes after a shock, describe the fault to a technician, and keep the appliance safe between services.
items.title: Water Heaters and the Electrocution Risk

items.summary: A medicine label tells you what is in the pack, how much is in one dose, and when to take it. After reading this you can read any medicine label in any country, measure a dose accurately, spot the instructions people most often ignore, and ask a pharmacist the questions that make the medicine work properly.
items.title: Understanding Medicine Labels and Dosage Instructions

items.summary: The nutrition panel is a set of numbers with a specific meaning, and the ingredient list is a set of names with a specific meaning. After reading this you can read any food label, judge a serving for yourself, compare two products fairly, check a claim on the front of the pack against the numbers behind it, and read a label with a specific medical need in mind.
items.title: Understanding Nutrition Facts and Food Ingredients

items.summary: Sleep is not lost time. It is when your body repairs, consolidates memory and regulates mood. After reading this you can judge whether you are actually getting enough, understand what your sleep cycle does, remove the habits that quietly break your nights, build a wind-down routine that fits a real week, and know when poor sleep needs a doctor.
items.title: Why Sleep Matters More Than You Think

items.summary: Doctors do not need more detail, they need better-arranged detail. After reading this you can describe a symptom so precisely that the doctor can narrow the cause quickly, answer the standard questions in full, and know when a symptom needs urgent care instead of a routine appointment.
items.title: How to Describe Symptoms to a Doctor

items.summary: Nam finds his grandfather's old bicycle with two paper wings taped to the frame, and it flies over the rooftops of the old quarter. Follow him past the lake, the wind and the moment he thinks he is lost. After reading, you can retell the flight, use five new words about flying in your own sentences, and say why the bicycle needed a second pair of hands.
items.title: The Flying Bicycle Adventure

items.summary: Hà finds a castle that only appears to children who come with empty hands, and she spends one whole day inside it. Follow her through the kitchen, the library and the garden, and to the great door with the small slot. After reading, you can retell the day, use five new castle words in your own sentences, and explain what the castle gave back.
items.title: One Day in a Magical Castle

items.summary: Bảo walks into a green valley where dinosaurs still walk, and finds something small under a big leaf. Follow her past the ferns, the giant footprints and the warm nests. After reading, you can retell the journey, use five new dinosaur words in your own sentences, and explain why she left the bone in the ground.
items.title: A Journey Through Dinosaur Land

items.summary: A boy finds an old green door in the garden wall and opens it into a garden that should not exist. Follow him past the ivy, through the hidden garden and to the surprise waiting at the end. After reading, you can retell the adventure, use five new garden words in your own sentences, and explain why he keeps the door a secret.
items.title: The Secret Door in the Garden

items.summary: Tuấn finds an old map in his grandmother's attic and walks across the hill to look for buried treasure. Follow him through three clues, a compass with a shaky needle and a long afternoon of digging. After reading, you can retell the hunt, use five new explorer words in your own sentences, and say what the real treasure was.
items.title: The Little Explorer and the Hidden Treasure

items.summary: A girl climbs into a rocket and flies all the way to the Moon. Follow her through the countdown, the long dark sky and the quiet grey surface. After reading, you can retell the trip, use five new space words in your own sentences, and explain why the Moon feels light and bouncy.
items.title: A Trip to the Moon

items.summary: A small robot called Bit leaves the workshop to find a friend, and nothing goes the way it planned. Follow him through the street, the rain and the park at night. After reading, you can retell the adventure, use five new robot words in your own sentences, and explain how Bit finally made a friend.
items.title: The Robot Who Wanted a Friend
